newsitem.title: DENMARK: Foreign predators threaten Danish insurers.
newsitem.headline: Foreign predators threaten Danish insurers.

text.p: Foreign insurance giants with sophisticated global networks are taking commercial trade from smaller Danish firms unable to provide the global service that the country's exporters demand, a broker said on Tuesday.
"There are few Danish insurance companies that can offer large exporters a global insurance scheme," Niels de Bang of Copenhagen-based AON Scandinavia, told Reuters.
"Many of the foreign insurance firms operating in Denmark in recent years use local brokers to find new clients. They need no organisation of their own," he said.
The traditional insurance company with an army of agents was being overtaken by smaller operations using brokers with good international links, he added.
"Close to 30 percent of Danish industrial insurance is handled by local brokers," he said.
AON Scandinavia is a unit of U.S.-based AON Corporation, the world's second biggest insurance brokerage.

"It is vital for insurance brokers and firms to be just as internationally orientated as the big industrial corporations. If an insurance firm is not part of a global network, it can still of course operate on a local basis," De Bang said.
"But it does not have the ability to offer the worldwide insurance programmes which companies with overseas subsidiaries are demanding more and more," he said, adding:
"The internationalisation of industry is threatening the existence of local insurers who cannot keep up and I think we are going to see many brokerages merging in the coming years."
Denmark's three biggest insurers, all have strong links with the global insurance network.

The biggest,Tryg-Baltica, is allied to Swiss Winterthur, Codan is majority-owned by Britain's Royal & Sun Alliance, and Topdanmark, Denmark's third biggest insurer, is connected to Dutch-based European group Eureko BV.

"Insurance brokers play a big role in the market, all the big insurance groups have brokerage sections. Competition within business insurance is intensifying with all the foreign firms now in operation in Denmark," an insurance analyst who wished to remain anonymous told Reuters.
"It is the small, non-stock exchange-listed brokerages which are going to suffer the worst," he said.
